**No, it isn't going as planned.** W0 is about two hours in against my guess of well under an hour. It is still making progress, so I'm leaving it running.

**Timeline (from the workflow journal):**
- **Baseline: about 60 minutes.** This was a cold debug build after the merge, and the e2e test binary took a long time to compile. The Haiku agent also thrashed: it killed and restarted its own builds several times.
- **Falsify: about 2 minutes.** It confirmed all 8 claims. That is fast and unanimous, so I spot-checked C4 and C1. Both had real evidence: C4 ran the actual plan command against `0e0016ed` and captured the rejection, and C1 traced the allowlist code and ran a real scratch-repo cargo run. No Opus escalation was needed. I'll still skim the rest of the evidence before trusting the ledger.
- **RED suite: about 58 minutes so far.** The implementer has made 56 Bash calls, and each cargo cycle takes about 5 minutes. It is actively iterating: a test run started at 15:11 is still going, so it isn't hung. It also created several new integration test files (`release_hardening_tests`, `release_plan_pypi_default_registry_test`, `cli_tag_template`, and others), and each file is a separate binary that must be compiled and linked, which adds to the cycle time.

**Estimate for the rest:** the implementer needs perhaps 15 to 30 more minutes. The reviewer then re-runs the crate suites plus the parked tests, likely another 20 to 40 minutes. Low confidence on both.

**Problem to know about:** the baseline agent ran `pkill -9 rustc`, which kills every rustc process on the machine. That could have killed builds in your other sessions if any were running (I saw peer sessions listed earlier). Worth a look if something died around 14:12 local time. I hadn't said "don't kill processes" in the workflow prompt, and I'll add that rule to every later one.

**Changes for the next workflows:**
- Have the implementer batch into one integration test binary instead of many. That cuts link time.
- Run `cargo test --no-run` once, then run only targeted tests.
- Have me run the heavy gates rather than paying for two agents to repeat them.
- Set a wall-clock limit per stage.
- Forbid killing processes the agent didn't start.

I'll report when W0 finishes. If you'd rather cut it short and review the partial test files now, say so.

content.text:
**You're right that this shouldn't take hours, and I found a likely cause.** It isn't the machine: 12 cores, load about 3, 162 GB free.

**What I measured:**
- **Feature sets flip between runs.** Different `-p` selections resolve different feature sets for shared dependencies, so cargo rebuilds them. I compared `cargo tree` for `callisto-cli`, `callisto-graph`, and `callisto-model + callisto-graph`, and the sets differ for `serde_core`, `rustix`, `futures-executor`, `getrandom` and `regex-syntax`.
- **The heavy rebuilds follow.** `serde_core` sits at the bottom of the tree, so a change there invalidates everything above it, including the `gix-*` crates. When I looked, rustc was live-compiling `gix_status`, `gix_merge` and `gix_blame`. The agents alternate `-p callisto-cli` and `-p callisto-model -p callisto-graph`, and each switch rebuilds a big slice of the tree. The audit agents did the same before, which fits the earlier 9 to 17 minute waits.
- **Not yet timed.** I haven't run a timed A/B, because the implementer holds the cargo lock now. I'd rate this as a strong explanation, not proven.
- **Right now** the implementer's `cargo test -p callisto-model -p callisto-graph ...` has been running for 11 minutes.

**On building and testing only at the end:** I'd keep some verification in the loop. Compiling and running tests is the only thing that proves a RED test fails for the stated reason, and if every failure surfaces at once, several will share the same cause. I'd change the cadence instead:

1. **One cargo invocation shape, always.** Use `cargo test --workspace` with test-name filters, so features never flip. The first run is cold. After that it is incremental.
2. **`cargo check` inside tasks, tests at gates.** Agents only compile-check while writing. I run the full workspace test at batch gates, not agents. That is close to your suggestion without losing the RED/GREEN proof.
3. **Fewer test binaries.** Put new tests in one integration binary. This W0 created many, and each one is a separate link.
4. **Permanent fix later:** a `workspace-hack` crate (cargo-hakari) makes every package selection resolve identical features. I'd propose it as its own small PR.
5. **Guardrails.** No process killing, and a wall-clock limit per stage.

**Decision for the running W0:** the implementer is probably near the end, but the reviewer stage will repeat the same alternation.
- **(a)** Let it finish. My guess is another 30 to 60 minutes.
- **(b)** Stop after the implementer's current cargo run and have me verify with one `cargo test --workspace` invocation, replacing the reviewer agent. The implementer's edits stay on disk, so nothing is lost.

I recommend (b). Say which and I'll proceed. I'll also time the A/B (`-p callisto-cli`, then `-p callisto-model -p callisto-graph`, then `-p callisto-cli` again) once the lock frees, so we know the actual saving.

entries.description:
- Stops a running background task by its ID
- Takes a task_id parameter identifying the task to stop
- To stop an agent-team teammate, pass its agent ID ("name@team") or bare teammate name as task_id
- To stop a background agent spawned with a name, pass that name as task_id
- Returns a success or failure status
- Use this tool when you need to terminate a long-running task

task_id.description: The ID of the background task to stop. Agent-team teammates and named background agents are also accepted by agent ID or name.

content.text:
W0 is done: I stopped the slow reviewer stage and verified the RED suite myself in one cargo run. The commit message is being drafted now, and I'll commit locally without pushing.

**Results:**
- **Falsification.** All 8 audit claims were confirmed with real evidence.
- **Suite passes.** The normal tests pass (exit 0): the 11 existing e2e tests unchanged, 21 new hardening tests, 5 new config tests, and 5 new model tests.
- **Defects captured.** 22 parked `red_*` tests all fail when run with `--ignored`. I read each failure message, and they match the stated defects:
  - **D01:** `cargo info` runs inside the workspace.
  - **D02:** `--repo` is rejected by both the strict fake `gh` and the real `gh api --help`.
  - **D03:** E167, the forge release isn't observed after creation, with a permissive `gh`, so the cause is isolated.
  - **D04:** E124, the trust evidence changes after `cargo publish`.
  - **D05:** the orchestration revision is validated after effects.
  - **D06 and D07:** the unconfigured profile without `[release]`, and the bare `product-package`.
  - **D08:** a receipt is issued although the remote never received the tag.
  - **Falsification claims C2, C3, C6, C7, C8:** covered, with 5 isolation-bypass tests for C8.
- **Test harness.** The shared fake-provider harness now has an opt-in strict `gh` that rejects unknown flags, and a knob for the real `target_commitish` shape. The old permissive behaviour stays the default so existing tests are unchanged.

**Gaps and open items:**
- **Missing tests.** Two claims have no parked test yet, because the implementer was cut off: C4 (recovery of a source without `[release]`) and C5 (yanked or already-published crates).
- **Clippy.** I haven't run `just lint` on the new test code. `cargo fmt` was failing on the new files, and I fixed it.
- **Startup delay unexplained.** The tests themselves run in about 12 seconds, but each new test binary took about a minute before starting, roughly 7 minutes of unexplained wall-clock. Re-running the same binaries took 6 seconds in total. I refuted two hypotheses: a fresh 1.2 MB test-binary copy started in 0.1 seconds, and a fresh copy of the large `callisto` binary in 0.5 seconds. It's unexplained, and I'll time each stage next run instead of guessing.
- **Build time.** The cold build in the single `-p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model` shape took 9m16s. Later runs should be incremental.

**Next:** W1 (design specs) has no cargo dependency except my gates, so it will run fast. Before that I'll add C4 and C5 tests as a small task, unless you'd rather fold them into the design work.

W1 (the design specs) is running. It is read-only apart from writing three spec files under `.claude/specs/`, so it doesn't touch cargo and shouldn't hit the build slowness.

**What it does:**
- **Architect A** (Fable/high): writes `SPEC-RELEASE-ENVELOPE-STATE`. It covers the persisted run envelope, canonical types, one observation type, and the state machine.
- **Architect B and C in parallel** (Fable/high, both reading A first):
  - `SPEC-RELEASE-PROVIDER-EXECUTOR`: the provider port, observe-decide-effect-confirm loop, timeouts, and the contract-test tier and fault-injection simulator.
  - `SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTE-SURFACE`: the typestate `execute`, profile authority, the `release candidate` and `matrix` commands, the workflow policy checker, and the traceability check.
- **Audit** (Sonnet): an auditor and a verifier per spec, plus a risk assessor on B.
- **Whole-system fit** (Fable/high): one `scribe:arch-auditor` pass across all three specs.
- **Correct and gate:** `scribe:drafter` (Sonnet) applies fixes, then an Opus/high exit-gate, with at most 2 rounds per spec.
- **Owner calls** (Sonnet/low): a final step lists every judgment-call criterion for you to accept or change.

**Ground rules I gave the agents:**
- **Recurrence prevention.** Every structural criterion must name its recurrence-prevention mechanism.
- **Acceptance oracle.** The parked RED tests are the acceptance oracle.
- **Provenance tags.** Every criterion is tagged user requirement, existing contract, external constraint, or judgment call. Your five recommended defaults (registry observation through the bound endpoint over HTTP, a generic `[release]`, the draft-then-publish GitHub Release flow, crates-only recovery of pre-`[release]` sources, and skipping `verify` on recovery) are marked as pending your acceptance.

I'll come back with the gate verdicts and the owner-call list, which is the stop point before planning.

| `SPEC-RELEASE-PROVIDER-EXECUTOR` (B) | 23 | 4 |
| `SPEC-RELEASE-EXECUTE-SURFACE` (C) | 30 | 6 |

The blockers fall into three groups:
1. **Scope.** All three are too big for one planning cycle. B admitted this itself and proposed a B1/B2/B3 split.
2. **Cross-spec contradictions.** The main one is what happens when a version already exists in an initial run (no `--recover` flag). A says `AlreadySatisfied`. B says `Blocked`, which contradicts the existing SRL-07 contract that an exact pre-existing effect is recorded as already satisfied. C and A also disagree on which registry keys the built-in coverage test iterates, and two specs both claim `is_managed_release_branch`.
3. **Provenance tags.** Five criteria are mislabelled, for example a `[UR]` tag on an item that is really a judgment call.

The gate is right about the scope, and more correction rounds won't fix it, since that is the loop your canon-pipeline notes warn about. The remedy is to slice the work, not to gate harder.

**Recommendation**
1. **Resolve the three contradictions in one targeted pass.** Adopt A's semantics (`AlreadySatisfied` on initial runs, `Adopted` on recovery runs). Fix the tags. Keep the specs `proposed`.
2. **Slice for build.** `navigator:planner` cuts the work into batches. Tier 1 is everything that turns the 22 RED tests green plus the structural core (envelope and state types, evidence-carrying observation, the provider port, the workflow fixes). Tier 2 is deferred as recorded follow-ups, per the CLAUDE.md deferral rule:
   - the data-driven target catalog
   - the module split
   - the fault-injection simulator's larger variants
   - the workspace-hack crate
3. **No more gate loops.** Each batch is accepted by executable checks (named RED tests green, contract tests) and my cargo gate.

**Two things I need from you:**
1. **Tag template.** Did you intend to rename the CLI tag from `callisto-cli@{version}` to `callisto@{version}`? If not, I revert it in one line and drop the `previous-tag-templates` machinery, and the installer issue disappears. If yes, that migration lands in Tier 2.
2. **Scope cut.** Is Tier 1 for this PR right, with Tier 2 as tracked follow-ups? I recommend it. A full build of all 80 criteria is likely many hours of agent time at current cargo speeds. I'll refine the estimate after planning.

**Engineering defaults I'd apply unless you object:**
- Registry observation over the profile-bound HTTP endpoint, with a neutral-cwd `cargo info --registry crates-io` as a fallback batch if HTTP slips.
- Draft, upload, then publish for GitHub Releases, with `--prerelease`.
- Crates-only recovery for a source without `[release]`.
- A targeted `recovery-checks` job instead of the full `verify`.
- Manifest schema bump and rename of `source_commit` to `coordinator_commit`.
- Plain `http` allowed only for loopback registry endpoints.
- `[release]` treated as Callisto-self for now, with one constants table that derives the workflow matrices.

---
name: cargo-slowness-target-pollution
description: Diagnosed root cause of hours-long cargo builds/tests in callisto (2026-09-18): polluted target/debug (1.7M .o files); fix, prevention, and the one-invocation-shape rule.
metadata:
  type: project
---

Cargo builds/tests took 9-60 min per run for weeks because `target/debug/deps` had accumulated **1.72M `.o` files (180 GB apparent)** since 2026-07-25. macOS dev profile defaults to `split-debuginfo=unpacked`, which keeps every codegen unit's `.o`; stale hashes are never garbage-collected. The same workspace built cold in a fresh target dir in **31 s** and ran 7 test binaries in **12 s** (vs ~7 min stalls before). Machine, disk, AV, Spotlight were ruled out by measurement (fs create 18k/s, stat 470k/s, same inside and outside the project).

**Why:** the user was rightly angry that "cargo should take minutes, not hours"; I had wrongly treated the slowness as normal for several hours and let agents pile builds on it.

**How to apply:**
- Before blaming the machine: `ls target/debug/deps | wc -l`. Healthy is roughly 10k. If above ~100k, `mv target/debug target/debug.stale` and delete it in the background, then rebuild (31 s).

content.text:
**Cargo is fixed.** The workspace tests now run in about 2 minutes. That is the cold build of the three crates plus 991 passing tests and 22 parked ones (0 failures), where graph alone used to take 17 minutes. It was measured while the old `target/debug` was still deleting in the background.

**Cause:** `target/debug/deps` had piled up 1.72 million `.o` files (180 GB apparent size) since July 25. macOS dev builds keep every codegen unit's object file by default, and stale ones are never garbage-collected. I had wrongly treated the slowness as normal, and I was wrong about that. What I ruled out by measurement:
- **Machine:** an M3 Pro on AC power with no throttling and load under 3.
- **Disk:** file-system speed is the same inside and outside the project.
- **Security or indexing agents:** none found.

**What I measured:**

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Cold build, 3 crates | 9m16s | 31s |
| 7 test binaries | ~7 min of stalls | 12s |
| Files in `deps/` | 1.74M | 1,074 |

**What I changed:**
- I moved the old `target/debug` aside and am deleting it niced in the background.
- I added a local `.cargo/config.toml` with `split-debuginfo = "off"`, excluded via `.git/info/exclude` so it isn't committed. In my measurement it produced zero `.o` files. It drops line-number debug info from macOS dev binaries. A repo-level setting would be your call.
- I saved the diagnosis and rules to memory: one invocation shape, no parallel builds, no process killing.

**Not done, so you know the state:**
- The three W1 specs are unaccepted and untracked in `.claude/specs/`. They are also larger than what we need, and I won't use them for gating.
- The RED suite is committed locally and not pushed. I'm not adding more tests.
- Nothing from the plan has been implemented yet. The 22 defects are all still open.

**Next, lean and with no more multi-agent pipelines.** I'd take the defects directly, in this order, with a targeted test run after each and one full run at the end (about 2 minutes now):
1. **P0s:** the `cargo info` cwd, the `gh api --repo` flag, and the forge identity via the tag-bound commit.
2. **Orchestration revision:** validate it before effects, and use `github.sha`.
3. **The target dir and trust check.**
4. **The workflow fixes:** timeouts, receipt upload, unused secrets.

Is that the right scope, or do you want the structural type work (envelope, evidence-carrying observation) included? I'd skip it for this PR and record it as a follow-up.

  (`prepared_tag_adapter_accepts_only_the_exact_intended_target`,
  `prepared_tag_adapter_rejects_conflicting_existing_target`) now drive `preflight_prepared`, which is
  where that decision moved. No new tests added.
  
  ## D04 — trust identity
  Test: `red_d04_two_crate_release_survives_cargo_leaving_a_target_dir` — un-ignored, passes.
  
  `GitCommitTrustEvidence::identity()` added in callisto-vcs (MIT, no new deps), returning a borrowed
  `GitCommitTrustIdentity { canonical_root, head, head_disposition }`. `PartialEq` on the evidence type
  is untouched, so no other user is weakened. Sibling sweep found three whole-value `!=` comparisons,
  all in release.rs, all switched to `.identity()`: `recheck_trust`, and both in
  `validate_release_intent_with_state_directory` (`trust != initial_trust`, `final_trust != trust`) —

  enumerating paths. The former `visited` set is renamed `on_path` and kept purely as the fail-closed
  cycle guard; a cycle's `false` is deliberately not memoized (it is a property of the path, not of the
  node), and any ancestor that inherits it memoizes `false`, which is still fail-closed. Existing
  semantics tests (`reconciliation_requires_transitive_exact_successes`,
  `direct_success_cannot_hide_an_unsatisfied_transitive_prerequisite`,
  `non_successful_or_attempting_prerequisites_never_make_dependents_eligible`) cover it and pass.

  New single source of truth `pub(crate) mod timeouts` in release.rs: PUBLISH 900s, REGISTRY_QUERY
  300s, ATTESTATION_VERIFY 120s, FORGE_API 60s, GIT_LS_REMOTE 60s, GIT_PUSH 120s,
  FORGE_RELEASE_CREATE 120s, FORGE_ASSET_UPLOAD 600s, LOCAL_GIT 60s. Routed:

  - `git push` → GIT_PUSH; `gh release create` → FORGE_RELEASE_CREATE; `gh release upload` → FORGE_ASSET_UPLOAD

    release_decision.rs `git_stdout`) → LOCAL_GIT
  - release_artifacts.rs now imports the shared `timeouts::ATTESTATION_VERIFY` instead of its private

fix(ci): make the release workflow a checked, bounded adapter

The release workflow resolved the orchestration revision from the moving tip
of main, so a push during verify made execute fail attestation verification
after a green run. A newer pending run could silently replace a queued release,
an unrelated pending changeset suppressed a release, recovery was blocked by
the full verify job, jobs had no timeouts, the receipt was discarded, and
execute held credentials it never used. The contract test was a set of line
greps that accepted every mutant tried against it.

Take the orchestration revision from github.sha and restrict the release path
to main, validate the dispatch SHA and the managed PR's head repository, add
per-job timeouts and per-SHA concurrency, gate recovery on a credential-free
check, upload the receipt, drop unused credentials, skip artifact jobs when the
plan has no slots, and add a parsed-YAML policy check that rejects each mutant.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01GiJEZewW2gKYPMeBgQBxZV
EOF
git log --oneline -1

**All 22 audited defects are fixed, in local commits on `codex/release-recovery`. Nothing is pushed.** The tests, clippy, fmt, the workflow linters, `callisto validate` and the workflow contract checks all pass on the final tree. The first real release still needs a GitHub run.

**The gate:** 1066 tests pass with none ignored, and the run takes about 40 seconds. Clippy, fmt, actionlint, zizmor, the pin check, the contract check, the new policy check (all 8 mutants rejected) and `callisto validate` are clean.

I also ran the exact command shapes the code now emits against the real providers, read-only:
- `cargo info` from a neutral directory with `--registry crates-io` finds the published `callisto-model@0.5.0` and does not find `0.7.2`.
- `gh api` without `--repo` returns 200 for a real release and 404 for a missing one.
- `git ls-remote` resolves a real tag.

**Five fix commits, plus your RED tests and a merge of `main`:**

| Commit | What it fixes |
|---|---|
| Provider observation | `cargo info` neutral cwd and explicit registry; one `gh api` helper without `--repo`; forge judged by tag name and draft state; tags observed on the remote via `ls-remote`; "already exists" text no longer counts as success |
| Executor | Attempting is persisted only before an effect; trust compared by identity, so the `target/` dir cargo leaves behind no longer aborts; every outbound command has a deadline; linear DAG reconcile |
| Config and tags | One canonical registry and repo destination; qualified `product-package`; manifest source-commit validation; pypi/nuget plan fallback; `previous-tag-templates`, so old `callisto-cli@*` tags stay found under your `callisto@{version}` tag |
| Workflow | Orchestration SHA from `github.sha` plus a main-ref guard; per-job timeouts and per-SHA concurrency; recovery gated by a credential-free check; receipt uploaded; unused secrets removed; retention 7 |
| Validation | Every input and the receipt path checked before the first effect; one profile authority (E198); a source with no `[release]` plans with zero artifact slots |

**Not verified until a real GitHub run:**
- the workflow's job graph and `always()` gating
- concurrency behaviour
- attestation verification against `github.sha`
- the `yq` path of the policy check
- the first real publish

**Deferred as tracked follow-ups:**
- the structural type redesign (envelope, evidence-carrying observation, provider port)
- the contract-test tier and fault-injection simulator
- the split of the 2000-line `release.rs`
- HTTP registry observation and yank detection
- PyPI observation
- Retry-After backoff

**My calls, for you to override:**
- **Isolation rule.** With no `production` profile configured, profiles are checked pairwise only.
- **`version-pr`.** It keeps `contents: write`, because it commits the managed branch.
- **Lightweight tags.** A lightweight remote tag counts as a conflict, and older tags like `callisto-vcs@0.2.0` are lightweight.
- **`verify` job.** It also runs on a dispatch with an empty input, because otherwise `release-candidate` never runs.

**Your call:**
1. **Push to PR #101?** I'll ask before pushing.
2. **Dry-run on GitHub.** I can dispatch a run to exercise the workflow graph. That is outward-facing, so also your call.
3. **Untracked files.** `.claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-*.json` and `.claude/plans/PR101-HARDENING/` are untracked. Keep them local or delete them?
4. **Incident report.** The 435-line incident report in the PR carries local paths and session IDs. Redact it or move it out of the public repo?
5. **Rotate `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`.** My env probe printed it earlier.

One mistake to own: my batch-3a commit skipped a new file (`git add -u` ignores new files), so it referenced a module that wasn't in it. I fixed that in local history and the final tree is identical to the one I gated.

Implement BATCH S1 (structural model core) of the Callisto release-lifecycle hardening in /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch codex/release-recovery; everything so far is committed). commit_authorized is false: do NOT commit or push. Be lean but complete: this is a structural change meant to make whole BUG CLASSES impossible or machine-detectable, not to patch instances.

BUILD RULES (a diagnosed slow-cargo problem; a full run of these crates is about 40 seconds, so if anything takes over 5 minutes something is wrong: stop and report): you are the ONLY cargo user. Always the SAME invocation shape: cargo test -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model -p callisto-vcs [--test NAME] [-- FILTER], GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/a08620cc-8b37-45b5-b4b2-89a977aad490/scratchpad/empty-gitconfig exported. Finish with cargo fmt --all, then the full test run, then cargo clippy -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model -p callisto-vcs --all-targets -- -D warnings. New files must be created normally (the caller stages them explicitly; list them in your report).

BACKGROUND: an adversarial audit found the release lifecycle repeatedly failed because (B) one fact has several authorities and provenance is assembled AFTER effects, (D) a provider "Exact" observation carries no evidence so "exists" is confused with "is the right thing", (E) operation state is mutated ad hoc so illegal orders (Attempting before observing) were representable. Reference material (read what you need): .claude/plans/PR101-HARDENING/audit/pr101-arch.md and pr101-core.md; DESIGN DRAFTS (proposed, not accepted, they contradict each other in places; follow THIS brief where they differ): .claude/specs/SPEC-RELEASE-ENVELOPE-STATE.json. Existing contract: docs/07-self-release-lifecycle.md, docs/specs/SPEC-SELF-RELEASE-LIFECYCLE.json (SRL-02, 06, 07, 08, 09). Current types: crates/callisto-model/src/release.rs (ProviderObservationV1 ~1824, OperationState ~1924, ReleaseExecutionStateV1 ~1867, ReleaseRunProvenanceV1 ~1755, ReleaseReceiptV1 ~2067), executor crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release_execution.rs and release.rs, state store release_store.rs, CLI crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs. crates/callisto-model is MIT: it must not depend on any other Callisto crate. Safe Rust only, atomic_write for persistence, terse one-line comments only for non-obvious WHY, no emojis.

DELIVER (all three parts, sequentially, tests green after each):

1. EVIDENCE-CARRYING OBSERVATION. Replace the bare ProviderObservationV1 { Absent, Exact, Conflict, Indeterminate } with Absent | Exact { evidence } | Conflict { reason } | Indeterminate { cause }. Evidence is a closed, per-role typed enum built from what providers can PROVE today: registry version (checksum and yanked as Option, filled where the provider can, None where it cannot yet), git tag (peeled commit), forge release (tag name, draft flag), artifact upload (size, sha256). Conflict reasons and indeterminate causes are closed enums derived from the cases the current provider code already distinguishes (tag points elsewhere, unannotated tag, forge release differs, asset differs, registry version exists but unobserved, provider status, command failure, malformed output, unsupported provider such as PyPI, timeout). An Exact evidence whose variant does not match the operation's role must be unrepresentable or rejected at the single constructor the receipt uses. The receipt's per-operation observations must carry the evidence (non-vacuous). Update the receipt wire schema version and the JSON schema snapshot/guard tests (see crates/callisto-cli/tests/schema_guard_test.rs and wherever schemars output is checked in) coherently. Provide two token types produced ONLY from an observation: AbsentProof (from Absent) and ExactEvidence (from Exact); later steps require them.
2. ENVELOPE FIRST. Extend/rename ReleaseRunProvenanceV1 to a run envelope (ReleaseRunEnvelopeV1: kind, orchestration revision, release-source revision, profile, intent digest, artifact manifest digest) that is created and validated BEFORE the first effect and persisted INSIDE ReleaseExecutionStateV1. The only constructor of a new execution state takes the intent AND the envelope (replace pending(intent)); loading/validating a state against the current run checks the envelope against the current run's envelope and against the intent, failing closed with a typed, actionable error when the state belongs to a different envelope (message says to use a new --state path or remove the stale state). Cross-field validity in the model: release-source revision equals the intent's source, intent digest and profile match, orchestration revision equals the artifact attestation policy's workflow commit whenever the intent has artifact slots, manifest digest is Some exactly when slots exist. The receipt is built from the state's envelope plus fresh evidence; remove the CLI's after-the-fact provenance assembly (crates/callisto-cli/src/commands/release.rs builds provenance around lines 400-430 after effects: it must now build the envelope up front and pass it in). One authority per fact: grep for every other place that derives or re-derives these values and route them through the envelope.
3. TRANSITION TABLE. Add one pure function on OperationState (or a small module) that is the ONLY way state changes: transition(current, event, run kind) -> Result<next, InvalidTransition>. Events cover: attempt (requires an AbsentProof), observed-exact-before-effect (Pending to AlreadySatisfied), confirmed (Attempting to Published, requires ExactEvidence), recovered-exact (Attempting to Published), effect-failed-and-absent (Attempting to Failed), blocked. Attempting must be unreachable without an AbsentProof (this is the structural guard for the earlier bug where Attempting was persisted before observing). Migrate the executor (release_execution.rs), reconstruction/recovery paths and the store so nothing assigns OperationState directly (grep the workspace, tests and fakes included). Keep Failed/Blocked variants and wire compatibility where possible, and keep existing behaviour: a real interrupted Attempting still fails closed on rerun, pre-existing Exact effects are AlreadySatisfied, Conflict/Indeterminate before an effect never persist Attempting. Add tests for the new invariants ONLY (small, at the public API): every (state, event, kind) triple against an explicit allowed list, bounded event sequences never reaching success without passing through legal edges, envelope cross-field validation (each field mismatch rejected), evidence-role mismatch rejected, state-with-other-envelope rejected on load. Existing tests must stay green; update expectations only where the intentional change (receipt schema, envelope) requires it.

Also: add a short .claude/semantic-model/release-lifecycle.md (terse, under 80 lines) describing envelope, observation+evidence, transition table and the E-codes involved, and add its row to .claude/semantic-model/INDEX.md.

FINISH: report files changed and NEW files, any deviation from this brief and why, and the PASTED final totals (passed/failed/ignored), clippy and fmt --check results. Do not report clean without pasted output.

content.text:
They differ only in coverage. `ci` runs fmt-check, lint, test, audit, doc-check, wasm-check and `coverage`. `ci-fast` is the same without `coverage`. The justfile comment says why the split exists:
- **CI parity.** Real CI already runs coverage as its own parallel job on a separate runner.
- **Cost.** Locally, coverage is a full-workspace recompile under `llvm-cov` instrumentation, tacked onto the end of a serial pipeline.
- **Purpose.** Coverage numbers are a reporting concern, not something every local run needs.

That reason is really a workaround for slow builds. The split was probably added when local cargo was already crawling, and the polluted `target/` I just cleaned up made every one of those recompiles worse. I haven't timed `just coverage` on the clean tree. `ci-fast` takes about 4 minutes.

If instrumented coverage now takes a few minutes, I'd collapse them into a single `ci`. Two names for nearly the same check invite people to run the weaker one and think they matched CI. I can time it after S1 finishes, since S1 holds the cargo lock, and then propose the change. Do you want that?

**Left out by choice:** the data-driven `[release]` catalog for other adopters, and the `workspace-hack` crate.

**Housekeeping needing you:** the push, the untracked spec and plan files, the incident-report redaction, and rotating `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`.

3. 3. Use it for provider-level tests of each outcome (Exact, Absent, yanked Conflict, 404, 429 then success with Retry-After, 5xx exhausting attempts, malformed body, cargo and PyPI paths). All existing e2e tests must pass unchanged in intent.
5. Update .claude/semantic-model/release-lifecycle.md (terse) for the new conflict reason and observation mechanism, and add a line to .changeset/release-product-artifacts.md if it is missing registry-protocol observation and retry.

- **S3:** the contract tier and fault-injection simulator, built on the new port.
- **S4:** the target-table drift test.
- **Sweeps:** installer verification, the hardcoded-values pass, and refreshing `docs/07` and the SRL spec, which S1 left describing the old model.

Implement BATCH S2c (GitHub Release draft, upload, publish) of the Callisto release-lifecycle hardening in /Users/gabe/Projects/callisto (branch codex/release-recovery; everything so far is committed, working tree clean). commit_authorized is false: do NOT commit or push. Be lean but complete.

BUILD RULES: you are the ONLY cargo user. ONE invocation shape: cargo test -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model -p callisto-vcs [--test NAME] [-- FILTER] with GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-gabe-Projects-callisto/a08620cc-8b37-45b5-b4b2-89a977aad490/scratchpad/empty-gitconfig exported. A full run takes about 40-60 seconds; if anything takes over 5 minutes stop and report. Never kill processes, never touch Cargo.lock or .cargo/config.toml, NO NEW CRATE DEPENDENCIES. Finish with cargo fmt --all, then the full test run, then cargo clippy -p callisto-cli -p callisto-graph -p callisto-model -p callisto-vcs --all-targets -- -D warnings. List NEW files in your report (the caller stages them). No test may contact the real network or GitHub.

WHY: today the forge release op creates a PUBLISHED release (gh release create --verify-tag --generate-notes, crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/provider/forge.rs) and product asset uploads happen afterwards. A published release therefore exists without its assets for the whole upload window, a failed upload leaves a published incomplete release, and with GitHub immutable releases (real releases now carry "immutable": true; cli/cli's do) assets can no longer be added after publication. The lifecycle contract says a release is complete only when registry versions, tags, GitHub Release, receipt and source commit agree, so PUBLISHING must be the LAST forge step, after every asset is uploaded.

  ## Design decisions
  
  **Model.** `ReleaseOperationRole::ForgePublish` added (wire `forgePublish`), with `ReleaseOperationId::forge_publish` / `ReleaseOperation::forge_publish` and `operation_id_text` -> `"forge-publish"` (so it enters the intent digest). `ReleaseIntentV1::SCHEMA_VERSION` 2 -> 3.
  
  **DAG.** `Tag` -> `ForgeRelease` (draft) -> every `ArtifactUpload` -> `ForgePublish`. `ForgePublish` is derived for *every* package that has a forge release, with prerequisites `[ForgeRelease] + all uploads of that package` — including the zero-upload case. Built in its own pass after the artifact-slot pass in `derive_release_inputs`, so it cannot miss slots. `canonical_operation_order` needed no change (generic topological sort).
  
  **Evidence.** `ProviderEvidenceV1::ForgeRelease` now serves both forge roles. `matches_role` became `check_role -> Result<(), EvidenceRejection>` so a `draft: true` release paired with `ForgePublish` is rejected by a *distinct* typed error, `ProviderObservationError::DraftReleaseCannotProvePublication`, rather than being folded into `EvidenceRoleMismatch`.
  
  **Prerelease.** One source: `Version::is_prerelease()` — the same call that computes the npm `next` dist-tag in `derive.rs`. It is read once per operation at derivation and carried on the prepared operations (`ForgeReleaseOperation`, `ArtifactUploadOperation`, `ForgePublishOperation` each gained `prerelease: bool`); no provider re-derives it.
  
  **Lookup.** `github_release_by_tag` is now private; `github_release_for_tag` is the one lookup all three roles share: tag endpoint first, then a bounded scan of `GET /releases?per_page=100&page=N` (max 10 pages, stops on an empty page). Both use the existing `retry_observation` + `timeouts::FORGE_API`. `malformed_github_response` extracted (artifact.rs was hand-rolling the same `ReleaseCommand` construction).
  
  **Observation.** Tag mismatch -> `ForgeReleaseDiffers`. Prerelease-flag mismatch -> new `ProviderConflictReason::ForgeReleasePrereleaseDiffers`. `ForgeRelease` is Exact for draft *or* published; `ForgePublish` is Exact only when `draft: false`, `Absent` while still a draft. Not found -> `Absent`. Both effects re-observe exactly as the other roles do; `ForgePublish`'s post-effect conflict is the new `RemoteConflict::ForgeReleaseNotObservedAfterPublish`.
  
  **Effects.** `gh release create TAG --repo R --verify-tag --draft --generate-notes [--prerelease]`; `gh release upload TAG PATH --repo R` (no `--clobber`, asserted by test); `gh release edit TAG --repo R --draft=false`. Provider selection stays in the single `provider_for` table.
  
  **Typed stale-intent failure.** `check_schema_version` now names found and expected. `read_intent` (callisto-cli) checks `schemaVersion` before serde and returns the new typed `CliError::ReleaseIntentSchemaUnsupported { path, found, expected }`, diagnostic code `callisto::release_intent_schema_unsupported`, whose help names `callisto release plan` as the fix.

  **A published release missing an asset uploads that asset; it is not a conflict.** Reasoning: the operation's identity is the *asset*, and `Absent` is the only observation that authorizes an effect in this model. Calling it a conflict would make an otherwise recoverable release permanently unrecoverable for the non-immutable case. On a real immutable release GitHub refuses the upload, which surfaces as the existing typed `GraphError::ReleaseCommand` rather than a release wrongly reported complete. 2. 3. STRICT BY DEFAULT: flip every fake tool in the harness (gh, git, cargo, npm) so unknown subcommands or flags FAIL with the real tool's style of message, using an explicit per-tool allow-list of the invocations the code legitimately makes; remove the legacy permissive default (keep an explicit opt-out ONLY if a specific existing test genuinely needs it, and name that test in your report). All existing tests keep their intent.
4. REAL-TOOL FLAG CONTRACT: add a test module that, for every external command shape the release path can emit (gh api / gh release create / edit / upload / gh attestation verify, git ls-remote / push / tag / rev-parse, curl, cargo publish, npm view / publish; find them by grepping the argv builders in crates/callisto-graph/src/commands/release/ and release_artifacts.rs and by reading the argv logged by the e2e harness), runs the REAL tool's --help for that subcommand and asserts every flag the code passes is listed there. The existing red_d02_every_emitted_gh_api_flag_exists_in_real_gh_help test in crates/callisto-cli/tests/release_hardening_tests.rs is the seed: generalize it into this module and delete the duplicate. Also add an end-of-test assertion helper in the harness that checks the argv logged by a full e2e run against the same allow-lists, and use it in the fresh-release, recovery and forge-publish e2e tests.
5. Update .claude/semantic-model/release-lifecycle.md with two terse lines describing the contract tier and how to refresh fixtures; add nothing to the changeset (test-only).

FINISH: report files changed and NEW files, which tools the flag-contract tests actually ran against on this machine versus skipped, any test that needed a permissive opt-out, and the PASTED final totals (passed/failed/ignored), clippy and fmt --check results, plus the output of running testing/refresh-provider-fixtures.sh's summary and just --dry-run provider-contract. 1. A SIMULATED WORLD implementing ReleaseProviderSet: per operation a remote state (Absent or Landed with typed evidence of the right role). observe(id) answers from the world; publish(id, proof) lands the effect if the world allows, refuses a duplicate landing the way real providers do (cargo/gh report already exists), and records every landing with its order. Faults are injected by a schedule keyed by call index: observation faults (Indeterminate; Conflict), effect faults (fails before landing; lands then returns an error, i.e. the response was lost; registry lag where the effect landed but the next N observations still answer Absent), and CRASH (process death) at any provider call or at any persistence point (before or after the k-th state save). 2. A realistic intent: about 2 packages with registry, tag, forge release (draft), 2 asset uploads, and the forge publish operation, using the real DAG derivation or the test-support builder so prerequisites are the real ones.

Faults are consumed (a fault budget of at most 2 per scenario) so a clean rerun is possible.
4. 5. PROVE THE SIMULATOR IS NOT VACUOUS: add tests that run the checker against deliberately buggy provider sets or writers (for example a provider that lies Absent after landing so a duplicate landing occurs; one that lands an effect ahead of its prerequisite; a state writer that loses the last save) and assert the corresponding invariant is reported as violated.
6. If the simulator finds a REAL violation in the production executor, providers or model, that is the point of this batch: reproduce it minimally, FIX it in production code with the smallest correct change (keeping every existing test green, no test weakened), and report each such bug with the scenario that exposed it. Do not weaken an invariant to make it pass; if you believe an invariant is wrong for a legitimate reason (for example registry lag semantics), say precisely why in your report and encode the exception explicitly with a comment.
7. Keep total added test time under about 20 seconds; state the scenario counts per category in the test output (print them with a stable prefix) and assert a minimum so a regression that silently shrinks the enumeration fails. Update .claude/semantic-model/release-lifecycle.md with two terse lines on the simulator and the invariants.

content.text:
About 2 to 2.5 hours of agent time is left, mostly sequential because only one agent can build at a time. Each batch takes 15 to 30 minutes, and my own gate adds about 2 minutes.

**Running now**
- **S3b (fault-injection simulator)** on Opus, roughly 20 to 30 minutes. It holds cargo.
- **Docs, installer and redaction** on Sonnet, roughly 15 to 20 minutes. It's in parallel because it needs no cargo. It covers:
  - refreshing `docs/07` and the SRL spec to the new model
  - attestation verification in the installer
  - stripping local paths and session IDs from the incident report

**Still to do, in order**
1. **S4:** the target-table drift test, about 15 minutes.
2. **Hardcoded-values and typed-error sweep**, about 25 minutes. It covers hardcoded values, `CliError::Other` in the release path, and the `recheck_trust` versus `recheck_git_remote` inconsistency.
3. **Full `just ci` with coverage**, 5 to 8 minutes, then an independent adversarial review (about 30 minutes) and its fixes (about 20 minutes).
4. **Decisions and outward steps, minutes on your side:**
   - your go-ahead to push
   - a GitHub dry-run of the workflow
   - the untracked spec and plan files
   - rotating `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN`

**What would cut it:** skip the adversarial review and the coverage-gate run. I'd advise against that, since the review is what would catch anything the batch gates missed. The sweep and S4 could also become follow-ups if you'd rather stop at "audited defects fixed plus the structural core."

  BATCH S3b complete. All tests green, clippy clean, fmt clean. Nothing committed (commit_authorized false).
  
  ## Design
  
  One in-crate `#[cfg(test)] mod release_simulator` in callisto-graph — chosen over an integration test because `VerifiedArtifactManifest`, `preflight_from_observation`, `release_test_support`, and `ReleaseOperationRole` pattern matching are all crate-private. It drives the **real** production path end to end: `execute_release` → `observe_release_operations` → `ReleaseReceiptV1::from_evidence`. Only a receipt counts as success, so the invariant checks cover the whole CLI success path, not just the executor.
  
  **Simulated world** (`SimWorld: ReleaseProviderSet`): per-operation remote is `Absent | Landed{evidence} | Conflicting{reason}`, with role-correct evidence from `release_test_support::evidence_for`. `preflight` routes through the *production* `preflight_from_observation`, and `publish` confirms by re-observing (never by an exit code), mirroring the real adapters. A second effect on a landed operation is refused the way cargo/gh refuse ("already exists"). Landing order and prerequisite state are recorded on every effect.
  
  **Simulated disk** (`SimWriter: ReleaseStateWriter`): writes to a real temp file so `ReleaseStateStore::load`'s `std::fs` read sees exactly what was durably saved; records every save's decoded operation-state map into the shared trace; can stop writing before or after the k-th save, retaining exactly the prefix.
  
  **Faults**: `ObserveIndeterminate`, `ObserveConflict` (permanent — the remote becomes a disagreeing object), `EffectFailsBeforeLanding`, `EffectLandsThenErrors` (response lost), `RegistryLag` (lands, next 2 observations still answer `Absent`). Observation faults are keyed by observation-call ordinal and effect faults by effect-call ordinal, so no scheduled fault is a no-op. **Crashes**: at any global provider call (an effect lands first — the harmless variant is already `EffectFailsBeforeLanding`) or before/after any save. Crash armed in run 0 only; faults armed in runs 0–1, so runs 2–4 are the three clean reruns convergence is asserted within.
  
  **Intent**: 2 cargo packages, 8 operations in real DAG order — alpha registry → tag → draft forge release → 2 artifact uploads → forge publish; beta registry → tag. Two artifact slots with a matching `ArtifactManifestV1`.
  
  **Reruns**: every scenario is run twice from scratch, once as M1 (same runner, persisted state, same Initial envelope) and once as M2 (fresh runner: state file deleted, Recovery envelope, reconstruction from observations).

  - one state-transition table
  - a provider port, with `release.rs` split into modules
  - registry observation over the crates.io sparse index and PyPI JSON API, with yank detection and retry that honours `Retry-After`
  - the GitHub Release created as a draft, with assets uploaded, then published last
  - captured real-provider responses, fakes that reject unknown flags, and flag checks against the real tools
  - a fault-injection simulator
  - drift checks for the target table
  - typed CLI errors
- **`just ci` is now the single full check.** `ci-fast` is gone, and coverage is included.

Two things still need real GitHub, which I can't do from here: the workflow's job graph and concurrency, and the first real publish. Nothing has run on GitHub yet.

1. **Push and update PR #101?** I'll ask before pushing.

content.text:
Two answers.

**Rebase: nothing to do.** Main hasn't moved. `origin/main` is at `341d7c93`, which is already inside the branch from the merge I pushed earlier, so the PR is 0 commits behind and mergeable. A real `git rebase` would rewrite 79 commits and drop 3 merge commits. It would need a force-push to the PR, and it risks conflicts replaying the original PR commits against main's licensing changes. It would gain nothing functional, since the PR is squash-merged. Say so if you still want it linearized. I'd take a backup ref first and use `--force-with-lease`.

**Installer "fail closed":** `setup-callisto` downloads a prebuilt Callisto binary from a GitHub Release and runs it on the CI machine, and it used to do that with no verification.
- **What I added.** After the download and before extraction, it runs `gh attestation verify` against `orin-dx/callisto` and the release workflow, so a tampered or substituted asset can't run.
- **What "fail closed" means.** If verification fails, or `gh` isn't installed, the step errors out. It doesn't continue and doesn't fall back to another install path. An escape hatch, `allow-unverified: true`, skips the check with a warning. It defaults to false.
- **Who breaks.** Only external repos that use the action's prebuilt-download path. Callisto's own CI builds from source, and its jobs passed. Releases built before this branch, such as `latest` or 0.5.0, have no attestation from the new workflow. So those repos would get a hard error until the first release built by the new workflow exists.

**Your choice:**
1. Ship it as is: most secure, breaks external users until the first attested release.
2. Default `allow-unverified` to true until then, then flip it: nothing breaks, but no verification for now.
3. **My recommendation:** if verification fails, don't run the downloaded binary and instead fall back to `cargo install` from crates.io, which checks its own checksums. That keeps the security property, since a tampered asset never runs, and doesn't break anyone. It costs a slower install on the fallback path. The action already has a crates.io fallback, so it's a small change.

Want me to implement option 3?

It's running on Sonnet with cargo banned. The design is one `verification` input on both setup actions:
- **`require`:** abort if verification fails or `gh` is missing, and never run the asset.

- **`skip`:** no verification, with a warning.

The wasm action has no source-install path, so its `fallback` behaves like `require` and says so. I'll verify it, commit, push, and watch CI when it reports.

content.text:
The installer's verification is now configurable, and **all 12 required checks pass on GitHub at `b52a00a7`**. The PR is mergeable and blocked only by the required code-owner review.

**What changed.** Both `setup-callisto` and `setup-callisto-wasm` take one `verification` input in place of the old boolean:

| Mode | On a failed or impossible verification |
|---|---|
| `require` | Abort. The asset is never extracted or run. |
| `fallback` (default) | Warn and delete the asset unrun. Then install from crates.io, keeping an explicit version pin. |
| `skip` | No verification, with a warning. |

The wasm plugin has no source-install alternative, so its `fallback` aborts. An invalid value fails immediately and lists the three valid ones. The docs and spec criterion AC-039 are updated, and the require-by-default alternative is recorded there as the rejected option.

**I also wired the installer tests into CI.** The 20, 3 and 15 installer test cases now run inside `just workflow-contracts`, which CI already runs. Before this they ran only by hand, so they would have rotted. They passed on the Linux runner.

**Side finding, not caused by this branch:** the other callisto-action test scripts (`test_status_check_branching.sh` and the rest, beyond the two CI runs) fail identically on a clean `origin/main`, and nothing runs them. They look stale. I left them alone; say if you want them fixed or removed.

**Rebase:** none needed. Main hasn't moved (`341d7c93` is already in the branch), so the PR is 0 commits behind.

Still open, and yours:
- the code-owner review
- the `orin-dx/actions` `rust-cache@v2` re-pin
- the bot-PR approval setting for release PR #99
- the 14 judgment calls in the new spec
- the token rotation, which is optional insurance

When a package version exists on registry, the result is `"failed:already-published"`. The code states: `if (result.result === "failed:already-published") { ... continue; }` — it skips silently without propagating as a hard failure.

**(3) Git tags creation:**

Yes, git tags are created. Timing: `"finally, create git tags as plan instructs"` occurs after all publishing completes. Successfully published packages are added to git tag releases: `gitTagReleases.push(...successfulNpmPublishes.map((result) => ...))`

**Retry**: Yes, for 2FA failures. Code loops: `while (result.result === "failed:needs-2fa") { ... result = await npmPublishQueue.add(...) }`

# Release Please Action Analysis

## (1) Action Outputs and Publication

**Outputs available:** `"release_created"` (boolean for root component), `"releases_created"` (boolean for any release), plus version details (`major`, `minor`, `patch`, `tag_name`, `html_url`, `upload_url`, `body`, `sha`).

**Publishing pattern:** Users create a separate conditional step: `"if: ${{ steps.release.outputs.release_created }}"` to trigger publication only when a release is created. The npm example shows checkout, Node setup, `npm ci`, and `npm publish` all conditioned on this output.

## (2) Concurrency, Re-running, and Recovery Guidance

**Not in this document.** No guidance provided regarding workflow concurrency, re-running failed workflows, or recovery procedures for failed tagging or release creation.

## (3) Detecting Merged Release PRs Requiring Tagging

**Not in this document.** The README explains that release-please maintains Release PRs kept up-to-date, and merging triggers releases, but does not explain the mechanism for determining whether a merged PR still needs tagging.

## (4) Token Permissions Guidance

**Required permissions:** `"permissions: contents: write, issues: write, pull-requests: write"`. 

Additional guidance: Users must `"specify a token for your workflows to run on Release Please's releases and PRs"` via a Personal Access Token instead of the default `GITHUB_TOKEN` to enable CI checks on release PRs, since `"events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run."` Repository setting: `"Allow GitHub Actions to create and approve pull requests"` may also be required.

I found relevant search results about handling already published versions with nx release and npm publish. Here's what I found:

## Key Findings:

**The Problem:** Running `npm publish` on an already-published version fails with a hard 403 error when re-running jobs, which prevents safe job reruns since the command fails before reaching any new packages that need publishing.

**Idempotent Publishing Solutions:**

1. **Skip Existing Versions:** The CI publish workflow can skip npm publication when the package version already exists on npm, making publishing idempotent and preventing 403 errors on re-runs.

2. **Nx Release Approach:** Nx Release provides a publishing subcommand (`nx release publish`) that performs just the publishing step for use in CI/CD pipelines.

3. **Idempotent Executor Design:** The publish executor can be designed to be idempotent so that reruns skip existing steps.

**Implementation:** The typical solution is to check if a package version already exists on npm before attempting to publish, then skip the publish step if it's already published. This prevents the 403 error that occurs when trying to republish an existing version.

title: Uploading assets to draft releases
---

If you need to upload assets to a release,
you likely want to create that release as a draft and only publish it once
you've uploaded the assets.

This recipe will show you how to configure Knope Bot to create draft releases
and provide a sample GitHub Actions workflow to upload and publish.

First, indicate to Knope Bot that there are assets to upload by adding the
`assets` config option to your `knope.toml` file:

```toml title="knope.toml"
[package]
# versioned_files and changelog config here
assets = "marker"

[bot.releases]

When ready, GitHub Actions calls into the `release` workflow which runs a single step: [`Release`].
This will compare the latest stable tagged release to the version in `Cargo.toml` (or any other `versioned_files`)

# Answers based on the immutable releases page:

**(1) What assets can be modified/deleted after publication?**

"Release assets cannot be modified or deleted" once published. The page states assets are "protected from modification or deletion."

**(2) Can a draft release have assets added or changed?**

Not on this page. The content discusses draft releases in the workflow context but doesn't specify whether drafts allow asset modifications.

**(3) Recommended workflow for immutable releases with assets?**

"Create the release as a draft. Attach all associated assets to the draft release. Publish the draft release." This workflow ensures "all assets are in place before the release becomes immutable."

**(4) What happens to the Git tag when immutable?**

"Once an immutable release is published, its associated Git tag is locked to a specific commit, cannot be changed, and cannot be deleted while the release exists."

# Rate Limiting Response Behavior

**(1) HTTP Status Codes and Headers:**

Status codes: "If you exceed your primary rate limit, you will receive a `403` or `429` response"

Headers to check: "the `x-ratelimit-remaining` header will be `0`" and you should "not retry your request until after the time specified by the `x-ratelimit-reset` header."

For secondary limits: "If the `retry-after` response header is present, you should not retry your request until after that many seconds has elapsed."

**(2) Secondary Rate Limits and Exponential Backoff:**

"If your request continues to fail due to a secondary rate limit, wait for an exponentially increasing amount of time between retries, and throw an error after a specific number of retries."

Based on the search results, here's what I found about GitHub Actions concurrency `queue: max` workflow syntax and changelog:

## Workflow Syntax

To allow multiple runs to queue instead of being canceled, set queue: max. With queue: max, up to 100 jobs or workflow runs can wait in the concurrency group; once the queue is full, any additional runs are canceled.

The queue: max option cannot be combined with cancel-in-progress: true, because the two options describe conflicting behaviors for handling in-progress runs.

## Changelog

You can now allow multiple jobs or workflow runs to wait in the same GitHub Actions concurrency group instead of being limited to a single pending run. Now, you can configure concurrency groups to queue multiple pending runs and process them sequentially, with support for up to 100 queued jobs or workflow runs per concurrency group. This update was announced in May 2026.

Increased queuing can be enabled by adding queue: max to the concurrency block in YAML when cancel-in-progress is false or not set.

## Processing Order

Jobs or workflow runs in the same concurrency group are processed in first-in-first-out (FIFO) order according to the time each one started waiting on the concurrency group.

content.text:
I have everything. CI on the latest push has 8 of 11 checks passed and the two test suites and coverage still running, so I'll flag that at the end. Here is the full result.

## What I fixed

1. **Package-name validation was rejecting real packages.** I ran our validator against 8,014 real names: the 5,000 most-downloaded PyPI projects, 1,037 crates and 1,977 npm packages. It wrongly rejected two classes that npm's docs allow: legacy uppercase names (`JSONStream`, `Base64`) and scoped names starting with `.` or `_`. It now rejects **0 of 8,014**, and the security rules (leading `-`, whitespace, control characters, `/ ? # % \`) still hold.
2. **Eight stale callisto-action tests are deleted.** I checked the cause: commit `c1adbf37` reduced that action to running the release-PR script, so the tests were extracting shell from steps that no longer exist. Nothing ran them.
3. **`plan-publish || true` in the validate action.** I tested it: `plan-publish` exits 0 on an empty plan and 1 on a real error. The last hosted run shows it succeeding and printing a real plan. So the `|| true` only hides genuine failures, and removing it is safe here. I did not change it. It's a required check, so blocking versus a warning annotation is your call.

## What the four tools actually do (read from their source and docs)

| Topic | changesets | nx release | knope | release-please |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Version already on the registry | Treats "previously published" as `failed:already-published` and continues (`npm.ts:290`) | Runs `npm view pkg@ver` first, skips: "already exists" (`release-publish.impl.ts:221,290`) | Doesn't publish to registries | Doesn't publish to registries |
| Network retry | None (only 2FA retry) | None | Exponential backoff, max 5, honours `Retry-After` (`http.rs:27-29`) | GraphQL 502 only, max 5 |
| Draft release, then assets | Publishes after `npm publish`, no assets | Creates or updates the release | **Draft, upload assets, then publish** (documented) | `draft` option, you upload |
| Release state | Git tags after publishing | Registry check | Tag comparison | Labels `autorelease: pending` then `tagged` |

I could not verify some things, so I'm not claiming them:
- The default `timeout-minutes` value.
- Any concurrency guidance in the changesets or release-please docs I checked.
- Cargo's `publish.timeout` key.
- Whether nx or knope have subprocess timeouts. Only my grep says no, and it is weak evidence.

## The 14 judgment calls

| AC | Call (our default) | Alternative | What the evidence says | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 016 | Registry observation by `curl` against the registry protocol | Use `npm view` or `cargo info`, or an HTTP crate | changesets and nx use the package manager. `cargo info` is what read our local manifest and can't see yanked versions. | Keep |
| 017 | 5 attempts, 2/4/8/16 s backoff, `Retry-After` honoured and clamped to 300 s | Other bounds, or none | Matches knope's retry policy and GitHub's rate-limit docs. One gap: for a primary limit GitHub says to wait until `x-ratelimit-reset`, and we clamp at 300 s, so a longer wait fails closed. | Keep |
| 018 | Receipt pass tolerates registry lag | Document the E174 dead end | `cargo publish` docs: the client "will poll waiting for the package to appear in the index, and may timeout". Lag is real. changesets and nx never re-check after publishing. | Keep |
| 019 | Per-command deadlines | One job timeout | None of the four sets per-command deadlines. GitHub kills a job at 6 hours. | Keep. Caveat: the `execute` job has never run in hosted CI (all 12 recent runs skipped it), so the 60 min budget and 900 s per publish are estimates. |
| 023 | Draft, upload, then a separate publish | Create published with assets | GitHub's immutable-releases doc: "Create the release as a draft. Attach all associated assets to the draft release. Publish the draft release." Assets "cannot be modified or deleted" after publishing. Knope documents the same flow. | Keep. Knope also passes `--latest` when publishing; we don't. |
| 027 | Source with no `[release]` plans crates-only with a notice | Reject it | No analog in the four. | Keep (needed to recover the 0.7.2 source) |
| 029 | Plain `http` only for loopback | https only | Not researched against these tools; they delegate transport to npm and cargo. | Keep |
| 030 | Per-ecosystem package-name grammars | Just add `--` to argv | None of the four validates names. Ours is now checked against 8,014 real names. | Keep |
| 038 | Per-SHA group, non-cancelling `execute` and `version-pr` groups | One group | GitHub docs: "any existing pending job or workflow run in the same group is canceled and replaced". See below. | **Change** |
| 039 | Installer: `require` / `fallback` (default) / `skip` | Require by default | `taiki-e/install-action` verifies SHA256 by default and has a `fallback` input (none, cargo-binstall, cargo-install; default cargo-binstall). `knope-dev/action` has no checksum or attestation strings. | Keep |
| 040, 041 | Captured fixtures, strict fakes, real-tool flag checks | Live integration tests only | No precedent found in the four. It's what would have caught the three P0s. | Keep |
| 042 | Bounded fault-injection simulator | Property or fuzz tests | No precedent found. | Keep |
| 043 | One Callisto-specific target table plus drift checks | Data-driven catalog | Knope is config-driven (`assets = "artifacts/*"`). This is the industry norm and our known deferred item. | Keep for self-release; the catalog comes later |

**038 is the one I recommend changing.** GitHub added `concurrency: queue: max` in May 2026 (I checked both the workflow-syntax docs and the changelog). It keeps up to 100 pending runs in FIFO order instead of replacing the older one, and it can't be combined with `cancel-in-progress: true`. A single per-ref group with `queue: max` would stop a queued release run being dropped, without per-SHA groups. The catch is that the latest actionlint (v1.7.12, March 2026) rejects the key, so we'd need a targeted ignore like the one we already have for `$/`. I'd do it with your OK.

## Three things beyond the 14 that the research raised

1. **Re-running `execute` after a partial release.** Changesets and nx both treat "already published" as success. We refuse it with E174 and only adopt in a recovery run. That is safer, but it makes a plain rerun impossible. A middle path: treat an existing version as already satisfied when the registry checksum matches the crate we packaged locally, and as a conflict otherwise. We already record the checksum. The risk is `cargo package` reproducibility across tool versions.
2. **Level-triggered release discovery.** Release-please rescans merged release PRs on every run, so a lost run heals on the next push. Ours triggers on one commit SHA. `queue: max` removes the dropped-run case but not automatic healing after a failure.
3. **Dry-run.** Nx and knope both treat `--dry-run` as a first-class flag. Our `plan` and `reconcile` are read-only, but `execute` rejects `--dry-run` by design.

**CI status:** the two fixes are pushed at `5267f45d`. 8 of 11 checks pass so far and the two test suites and coverage are still running. I haven't seen a failure.

**Your decisions:**
- adopt `queue: max` (with the actionlint ignore)
- make `plan-publish` blocking or warning-only
- take on any of the three extras
- accept or change any of the 14 calls

Sources: [GitHub immutable releases](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/concepts/supply-chain-security/immutable-releases), [rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api), [workflow syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax), [actions limits](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/limits), [concurrency-queue changelog](https://github.blog/changelog/2026-05-07-github-actions-concurrency-groups-now-allow-larger-queues/), [cargo publish](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-publish.html), [npm name rules](https://docs.npmjs.com/cli/v11/configuring-npm/package-json#name), [knope](https://github.com/knope-dev/knope), [changesets](https://github.com/changesets/changesets), [nx](https://github.com/nrwl/nx), [release-please](https://github.com/googleapis/release-please), [taiki-e/install-action](https://github.com/taiki-e/install-action).

content.text:
The batch is running on Opus. It replaces curl with the package manager, drops http entirely, and refuses PyPI at plan time, and I'll gate it as usual when it reports. The design decisions it carries:

- **Cargo:** `cargo info NAME@VER --registry X` runs from the workspace root, so it uses the same `.cargo/config.toml` registry definitions and credentials as `cargo publish`. That is your auth point: private registries just work, and we reimplement nothing. Exit 0 with a matching `version:` line gives Exact. Exit 101 with the exact "could not find `NAME@VER`" phrase gives Absent. Anything else is treated as transient, so a network failure can never read as Absent.
- **Yanked crates:** they read as Absent because `cargo info` can't see yanks. That fails closed, since the next `cargo publish` is refused and surfaces as the existing unconfirmed-publication error.
- **npm:** unchanged.
- **https only:** no loopback exception, and the same check is used at config load and release binding.
- **PyPI:** refused at plan time with a clear reason. pip can't tell a missing project from an unreachable index, so guessing would be unsafe. The durable release path is new, so nothing existing breaks.
- **Tests:** real `cargo info` runs against a hermetic local registry with no network, plus captured real cargo and npm outputs as fixtures. Together they prove the original defect stays fixed: with an explicit `--registry`, the local workspace manifest is never read.

If you'd rather support PyPI some other way, tell me before this lands.

content.text:
The S6 change is committed and pushed (`99546e75`), and CI is running on GitHub. The background wait will tell me when it settles.

**What S6 did:**
- **cargo:** observed with `cargo info NAME@VER --registry X` from the workspace root, so it resolves registries and credentials the same way `cargo publish` does. Only the exact "could not find `NAME@VER`" message counts as absent. A network failure is never read as absent.
- **npm:** unchanged.
- **PyPI:** refused at plan time with a typed error explaining that pip can't tell a missing project from an unreachable index.
- **Registry endpoints:** https only, with no exception. No `curl` remains in the Rust code.
- **Tests:**
  - Sixteen run the real `cargo` against a hermetic local git registry, with no network.
  - Captured real cargo and npm outputs are fed to the classifiers.
  - One test proves the original defect stays fixed: without `--registry` cargo reads the local workspace manifest, and with it it doesn't.
- **Yanked crates:** the real-cargo run confirmed the yanked case. A yanked version reads as absent, with the same "could not find" message. That fails closed, because the next `cargo publish` is refused.

**Local gates passed:** 1151 tests, clippy, fmt, rustdoc and the workflow contracts.

**Two small notes:**
- Each full local test run leaves about 2 small directories (about 52 KB each) under `~/.cargo/registry/index/`. It's harmless, but I can make it deterministic if it bothers you.
- One enum variant, `RegistryVersionYanked`, is now produced by nothing. I left it in the wire enum to avoid another schema change.

I'll report the CI result when it lands.

content.text:
Not super confident about the first real release. I'm confident about the code, and there is a gap that only a real run can close.

**High confidence, because it was executed or measured:**
- **CI on real runners.** All 12 required checks pass on GitHub across Linux and macOS: 1,544 tests, coverage at 92%, all four artifact builds, and the workflow policy checks. The last local `just ci` also passed.
- **The release logic.** I ran a simulator that crashes the real executor at every persistence point and injects provider faults, and it found no violations. I also checked our parsers and validators against captured real responses from cargo, npm, GitHub and git, and against 8,014 real package names.
- **The `gh` draft flow.** I just read `gh`'s own source. `gh release upload` calls `FetchRelease`, which finds "a draft release by its pending tag name", so uploading to a draft by tag works. This is source reading, not a live run.

**Not proven, and the reasons are concrete:**
1. **The release workflow has never run for real.** It only triggers from `main`, and every recent release run skipped the `execute` job. Its job graph, concurrency behaviour and attestation-against-`github.sha` check are verified only by linting, policy mutants and reasoning.
2. **The GitHub write path has only run against fakes.** Creating a draft, uploading assets and publishing were tested with fakes shaped from real read-only responses. Nobody has run them against a real repo.
3. **The 60-minute `execute` budget and the 900 s per publish are estimates.** I have no timing from a real run.
4. **Attestation verification against a real asset** can't be exercised until a release built by the new workflow exists.

**Where I was wrong along the way,** which is why I don't trust my own reasoning without a check. I withdrew the license finding, treated the slow cargo as normal for hours, missed a file in one commit, and first wrote package-name rules that rejected real npm packages until the corpus check caught it. Each time, what I had measured held up better than what I had only reasoned through.

To close the biggest gap, run the workflow's GitHub side end to end (draft, upload, attest, publish, job graph) in a scratch repo. `orin-dx/callisto-rehearsal` is reserved for exactly this. It can't rehearse crates.io publishing. Shall I set that up?

content.text:
The first real release is next, and it's ready. I rehearsed everything I safely could and nothing failed.

**After your merge:** the release workflow ran on `main` and did what it should. `verify` passed, it correctly decided this wasn't a release-PR merge, and it updated the managed release PR (#99). The `plan`, `build`, `assemble` and `execute` jobs were skipped, so nothing was published.

**What release PR #99 proposes:** it bumps all 10 crates from 0.7.2 to 0.8.0 across 24 files, including changelogs, `Cargo.lock` and the release decision file. Merging it publishes 9 crates to crates.io and creates the GitHub Release for the CLI.

**Read-only rehearsal, all clean:**
- I simulated the squash-merge in a scratch worktree, which I've removed, and ran the real `release plan`. It produced a valid intent: schema 3, 24 operations, the four artifact targets, profile production.
- `release reconcile` works.
- Against the real providers, none of the nine crates has 0.8.0 on crates.io, and there are no 0.8.0 tags or releases, so nothing conflicts.
- All nine crates already exist on crates.io, so these are ordinary new versions. The crates.io API shows them owned by your account (`castrog`).
- The `CARGO_REGISTRY_TOKEN` org secret exists and is visible to this repo.
- One rehearsal hiccup, my own doing: `plan` first failed with E051 ("ignored path outside its fixed allowlist"). The cause was `.entire/logs/`, which your local Entire hook writes when I made the scratch commit. Hosted runners don't have that hook.

**The blocker:** PR #99 has zero checks and is blocked on review. The bot-authored PR triggers none of the 12 required checks. Your account is a bypass actor on the `main` ruleset with mode "always", so you can merge it directly. That is the documented path today, but it means the sole release authorization skips the required checks.

**Your decision:**
1. **Merge #99 now with your bypass (my recommendation).** The release then runs unattended: `plan`, four artifact builds, attestation, then `execute`. I'll watch it, and I have the recovery path ready (`workflow_dispatch` with `release_source_sha`).
2. **Fix the checks first.** Create the release PR with a PAT or App token instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN`, then merge normally. It's cleaner, but it adds a new secret and policy change and delays the release.
3. **Rehearse the GitHub side in a scratch repo first.** It can't rehearse crates.io.

**Risks you should accept knowingly:**
- Publishing to crates.io is irreversible. You can yank a version but not delete it.
- The `execute` job has never run, so the 60 minute budget is an estimate.
- I can't check that the token is unexpired and correctly scoped. If it isn't, the first `cargo publish` fails before anything is published, and recovery is safe.

Which option?

git add .github/workflows/callisto-ci.yml .github/workflows/callisto-release.yml && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
ci: install just from a checksummed manifest instead of the releases API

The macOS test job on main failed at setup-just with "GET
/repos/casey/just/releases - 500": setup-just resolves the version through
the GitHub releases API and does not retry, so one transient server error
fails the job before any project code runs.

Install just through taiki-e/install-action, already pinned in these
workflows. It downloads a direct release URL with curl --retry 10 and verifies

I fixed the cause in PR #102 and I'm waiting on its CI. **The cause:** `extractions/setup-just` looks up the `just` version through the GitHub releases API and never retries. One transient GitHub 500 therefore failed the macOS job before any of our code ran.

**Fix, in two parts:**
1. **The failed run on `main`.** I re-ran only the failed job, and that result is included in the check I'm running now.
2. **The cause.** PR #102 replaces all eight `setup-just` steps (six in CI, two in the release workflow) with `taiki-e/install-action` (`tool: just@1.58.0`). It's the action we already pin in those files. I read its source. It downloads a direct release URL with `curl --retry 10`, so there is no API lookup to fail. It also checks a SHA256 for each platform from its manifest, so the binary is integrity-checked. The `just` version stays 1.58.0.

**Checked locally:** actionlint, zizmor, the pin check, the release workflow contract and policy checks, and all 25 self-test mutants. The real proof is that PR's CI, because those steps only run on GitHub's runners. I opened #102 as a normal PR, so it needs your review or bypass to merge, same as the others.

**What it doesn't cover:** `moonrepo/setup-toolchain` and `orin-dx/actions/setup-rust` also download from GitHub. They weren't the failure here, so I left them alone. If they flake the same way, the fix is the same: rerun, and look for a retrying installer.

The release is unaffected. It runs in a separate workflow that already succeeded, and it is still waiting on you to merge PR #99. I'll report both results when the checks finish.

The design removes that failure mode: there is no unretried API call, and the download has `curl --retry 10` and a checksum.

- **PR #102** (the durable fix for that flake): ready for your review or bypass.
- **PR #99, the release PR:** still open. Merging it is what starts the release, and nothing has been published yet.

**Next, in order:**
1. Merge #102, so CI is more robust before the release run.
2. Then merge #99 with your bypass (option 1 from before), or pick the alternatives (fix the release-PR checks first, or rehearse in a scratch repo).

I'd merge #102 first. It costs one merge and removes a known flake from the workflows the release will run through. Do you want to merge #102 and then #99?
